timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Alrighty.
Hello, this is Colleen Chumaker with the League of Women Voters of Portland and you are
watching the Video Voters Guide.
We in conjunction with Metro East Community Media are here to talk with candidates running
in the May 2020 primary election.
With me today is Julia DeGroff running for Portland City Commissioner position 2.
Welcome Julia.
Hello, thanks for having me.
Please tell us a little about yourself while you are running for this office and what
unique characteristics you have among all the candidates for this office.
Yeah, definitely.
Again, my name is Julia DeGroff and I am running for Portland City Council position 2.
I ran for this seat a couple of years ago in 2018 on a system change platform.
I have a 15 year career in the nonprofit sector doing a lot of campaign and policy work.
It included a nine year fight to keep a Nestle Water Bottleing facility out of the Columbia
River Gorge.
It also included doing a lot of policy work at the municipal and state level and with the
city of Portland that meant engaging on a number of water related issues.
I really became aware of the dysfunction of the commission form of government in my opinion
and the inequities of electing people through citywide elections.
I really campaigned on the need to elect folks from across the city, from city council districts
to increase representation on council and to have elected officials who are more focused
on creating policies and finding the solutions to our biggest long term problems rather than
the day-to-day operations of bureaus.
So that was really my drive for running the first time and I think that those issues are
as if not more relevant now than they were two years ago after the seat club report came
out and even the League of Women voters has done a report on this issue.
We're heading into a charter review year and I'm the candidate you want in that seat
who understands the system as it is, can operate in the system as it is as well as possible
but who is ready to engage in a deep community engaged process to head into a charter review
process that leads to system change.
So that's why I'm running.
Thank you.
The COVID-19 pandemic and the resulting devastation of small businesses, city employee layoffs
and housing displacement will be with us for some time.
How would you seek to address the fallout including the reduction in city revenue?
Yeah, this is frankly because of a lot of the major issues with the commission form of
government and other revenue issues that pre-existed before COVID.
We already had some very large systemic problems.
The housing crisis was already a crisis before we had a pandemic on our hands.
What I've been saying from the beginning of this campaign and something that I think
makes me sound out against other candidates who are running for this seat is I really
talk about our problems as they, in a systemic way, I don't talk about them in isolation
one from the other because they're generally related to each other.
We need to work collaboratively across bureaus and across the commissioners and across jurisdictions
to address these large systemic problems and that is particularly true with COVID, with
responding to this crisis.
Unfortunately, we can't be expecting to get the kind of major resources we should be
getting from the federal government in order to make sure that our small businesses have
the money that they need to keep people on payroll.
So what I would be recommending at this time is that municipalities like Portland and
up to the state of Oregon dip into our reserves that are there for emergency situations to
create, to fund all the local businesses with the stipulation that they keep people on payroll
because they need that assistance yesterday.
They need that assistance.
I mean, most small businesses don't have more than a month or so of operating money in
their bank at any given time.
They're not going to withstand this shutdown if we don't get money in their hands.
And Portland, more so than other cities across the United States, is a small business town.
The employee over half the employees in our city and we need to act quickly to keep them
afloat.
And again, there's, so now I would also recommend using reserve funds for keeping parks and
other things that operate more on fees and the usage of the public.
We need to dip into reserve funds to keep those afloat as well because that's going to
be what it takes in order to keep this from becoming a much longer term depression era
situation.
If we maintain our current government structure, what city bureau would you want to oversee
and why?
So we're going to maintain this at least through 2020.
So we are going to have a try to review process that I'm very excited about engaging in
and engaging the community in.
However, for that duration where we're going to continue to have this form of government,
there are a number of bureaus I'm interested in.
But I think the one that makes the most sense and is my number one choice is the water
bureau and environmental services.
My career has been spent working on environmental issues and particularly with a focus on water.
I've been invited to give expert testimony on water issues as a professional when I was
the senior organizer at Food and Water Watch.
A really deep policy background there and I think that I could hit the ground running
with that position and then be able to support other commissioners on other issues that
are near and dear to my heart like working with Joanne, Commissioner Hartisty, excuse me,
police accountability like everyone is doing on council right now and working with
Chloe, Daily's office on really revolutionizing our transportation department to get us on
track for carbon emission reduction.
Thank you.
You already alluded to this but how would you address the public significant concerns about
police and community relations, the use of deadly force and officer accountability?
Yeah, this is something I campaigned on last time as well.
It's a huge issue and according to the police, the police, their own data, their own report,
over 70% of Portlanders don't trust the police right now.
That's a complete breakdown in trust and I really believe that trust is predicated on accountability.
We need to be able to see that officers are held accountable to excessive force, to racial
profiling and we've had, we've just seen too many examples of that not happening, of accountability
not occurring in the police force and that's why this trust is dwindling.
I think one of the major priorities is getting a more community-centered police contract.
I've been working on that over the last year as the executive director of Portland forward
and on the steering committee of Portland Metro Peoples Coalition, I was working with
a network of organizations that were really trying to keep the pressure up and the process
for the negotiation of the new police contract to get more independent community oversight built
in to just build in a lot more community-centered and accountability prospects within the contract
with the PPA.
Between negotiations though of this contract, we're going to have to continue working on this
because we're not going to solve all these problems from one renegotiated contract.
We're going to have to continue working on policies that improve community oversight and
accountability with the police so we can start restoring that trust.
And I also believe that part of that includes having a much less militarized response to
protest in the streets but we have a short time for answers so I'm going to leave it at
that.
Well, thank you.
That's actually all we have time for.
So thank you very much for coming out today.
And this has been the Video Voter's Guide.
Thank you for watching.
The primary election is Tuesday, May 19.
Be sure to inform yourself about the candidates and the ballot measures and exercise your right
to vote.
